title: Half of Bangladesh's poorest households get no safety net: World Bank
excerpt: The country spends 3.5% of GDP on subsidies and social protection, but richer families capture much of it while poverty rises.
content:
Research summary · Poverty and social protection · Source: World Bank, October 2026

Bangladesh spends about 3.5% of GDP (US$17.4 billion) a year on energy and fertiliser subsidies and social protection, yet half of the poorest households receive no safety net support at all, according to the World Bank’s Bangladesh Development Update for October 2026. Its special focus, Make Subsidies and Social Protection Work Better for the Poor, finds that much of the money reaches better-off families.

The findings come as poverty rises. The Bank’s Poverty and Equity Brief for October 2026 says the country’s “prolonged slowdown is pushing households back into poverty”, with over a third of the population living just above the poverty line.

Poverty is rising for a fourth year

  • At the international line of US$3.00 a day (2021 prices), poverty is estimated to have risen by 1.1 percentage points to 10.1% in fiscal year 2025-26 (FY26, July to June). That is about 2.1 million more people in poverty than in FY25.
  • At the national poverty line, the Bank estimates poverty at 22.5% in FY26, up from 18.7% in the 2022 HIES. Prothom Alo and The Business Standard report that the Bank projects 22.8% in FY27.
  • GDP growth was 3.4% in FY26 and is forecast at 3.4% again in FY27. Average inflation eased from 10.0% in FY25 to 8.7% in FY26 but is projected to stay high, at 8.6%, in FY27.

These poverty figures are World Bank model estimates. They are not results from a new official household survey, as The Financial Express has noted. The Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) has not released a household survey since 2022.

Where the subsidy money goes

Total subsidies rose from 0.9% of GDP in FY14 to 2.2% in FY25, driven mainly by electricity and energy. Power and gas subsidies grew from Tk 85.8 billion in FY14 to Tk 836 billion (1.5% of GDP) in FY25. Fertiliser subsidies rose from Tk 72 billion in FY20 to Tk 280 billion (0.5% of GDP) in FY25.

The table shows the trade-off the report describes. Richer households capture more of the money, so subsidies are a costly way to help the poor. But the support is a large part of poor families’ income, so cutting it without compensation would hurt them. The Bank estimates that removing electricity subsidies in full would raise poverty by 2.8 percentage points, or about 4.7 million people.

Gaps in social protection

  • Broad social protection spending was 1.9% of GDP in the FY26 budget. The FY27 allocation is Tk 1.44 trillion, or 2.1% of GDP.
  • Government employee pensions and agricultural subsidies take about 43% of the social protection budget. The 48 programmes the Bank classes as pro-poor get about 39%.
  • Pro-poor programmes miss 63% of households in the poorest fifth and include 18% of households in the richest fifth.
  • The poorest 40% received about 44% of social assistance benefits in 2022, down from 51% in 2016.
  • Social protection cuts poverty by 3.05 percentage points, below the average of 3.89 points for lower-middle-income countries.

The report also warns of a new cost pressure. If the new government pay structure is fully implemented, pensions could rise by about 70% and basic salaries and allowances by about 120% on average, adding about 0.6% of GDP to spending in FY27, Prothom Alo reported.

What the Bank recommends

  • Better targeting with the Family Card. In its first phase the card covers 4.1 million households with Tk 2,500 a month. The Bank estimates this cuts poverty by a further 0.95 percentage points (about 1.58 million people). Cutting inclusion errors by a quarter would raise that to 1.25 points (2.07 million people) at no extra cost.
  • Consolidate food programmes. Combining the Family Card with better targeting and consolidation of food programmes such as Open Market Sale and Vulnerable Group Feeding could lift about 2.85 million people out of poverty. Spending would rise by 0.21% of GDP, to 1.78%.
  • One registry. Link the Family Card, the Dynamic Social Registry (DSR), the Farmers’ Card and other beneficiary databases to find overlaps and gaps. The DSR rollout is planned by June 2028.
  • Electricity tariffs. The average tariff is Tk 10.63 per kWh against a cost-recovery level of Tk 15.16. The Bank proposes a lifeline rate for the first 75 kWh, block pricing above it and no subsidy above 150 kWh. It estimates this would save about 0.4% of GDP with little change in poverty.
  • Fertiliser. Raise prices in small, phased steps and move the savings into research, extension and irrigation.

Why it matters

For NGOs, the numbers describe the households many programmes already serve: poor families outside every safety net, and some 62 million people living just above the poverty line, as The Business Standard reported from the Development Update. The Family Card rollout and the DSR will decide who is eligible for government support in the coming years, so organisations that help people register, check lists or handle complaints will have a direct role. Donors funding cash transfers and shock response can push for links to the same registry, so programmes do not overlap.

Limitations

The incidence analysis uses 2022 survey data, before the recent rise in poverty and the start of the Family Card. Poverty figures for FY26 and later are model estimates. The reform results are simulations that assume good delivery, which past targeting problems suggest is not guaranteed.

What to watch

  • Whether the government links Family Card lists to the DSR, and how it handles appeals from excluded households.
  • Any electricity or fuel price changes in the coming months, and whether compensation for poor households is announced with them.
  • Whether BBS schedules a new Household Income and Expenditure Survey to test the Bank’s poverty estimates.
